summary: In the temple, the angel Gabriel tells the aged priest Zacharias that his barren wife Elizabeth will bear a son, John, who will prepare the way for the Lord.
key_insight: The prophets close with Malachi’s promise that Elijah would come to “turn the hearts of the fathers to the children” (Malachi 4:6). Gabriel takes up those very words. After some four hundred years with no new prophetic book, God resumes His story exactly where Malachi left it.
story: In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zacharias, of the division of Abijah. His wife Elizabeth also came from a priestly family, one of the daughters of Aaron. Both were righteous before God, “walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless.” But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were well advanced in years.

When Zacharias’s division was on duty in the temple, the lot fell to him to go into the temple of the Lord and burn incense. Outside, the whole multitude of the people was praying at the hour of incense. Then an angel of the Lord appeared, standing on the right side of the altar of incense. Zacharias was troubled, and fear fell upon him.

The angel said, “Do not be afraid, Zacharias, for your prayer is heard; and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.” The child would bring joy and gladness to many. He would be great in the sight of the Lord, drink neither wine nor strong drink, and be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb. He would turn many in Israel back to the Lord their God and go before Him “in the spirit and power of Elijah,” to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.

Zacharias asked, “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is well advanced in years.” The angel answered, “I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God, and was sent to speak to you and bring you these glad tidings.” Because Zacharias did not believe, he would be mute until the day these things took place.
Outside, the people waited and marveled that he stayed so long in the temple. When he came out, he could not speak to them. He kept beckoning to them, and they realized he had seen a vision.

When his days of service were over, Zacharias went home. Soon afterward Elizabeth conceived, and she hid herself five months, saying, “Thus the Lord has dealt with me, in the days when He looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.”

scene.label: The division of Abijah
scene.text: David divided the priests into twenty-four divisions, and Abijah’s was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:1–19). Each division served in the temple for a week at a time, about twice a year, and all the priests served together at the great feasts.

scene.label: The lot for incense
scene.text: Priests drew lots for each day’s duties. Burning the incense inside the Holy Place was the high point of the service. With so many priests, later Jewish writings say a man could do it only once in his life. This was probably Zacharias’s one day.

scene.label: The hour of incense
scene.text: Incense was burned every morning and evening (Exodus 30:7–8). While the smoke rose inside, worshipers prayed in the courts outside. Incense was a picture of prayer: “Let my prayer be set before You as incense” (Psalm 141:2).

scene.label: Childless in Israel
scene.text: Childlessness was a deep grief and often a public shame, which is why Elizabeth speaks of her “reproach.” Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah had all waited for sons God gave. When Rachel’s son was born she said, “God has taken away my reproach” (Genesis 30:23).

scene.label: Gabriel
scene.text: Gabriel had come to Daniel “about the time of the evening offering” (Daniel 9:21), with a message that looked ahead to “Messiah the Prince” (Daniel 9:25). He appears again at the hour of incense, now to say that the time has come.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke tells of John’s birth. He begins his Gospel in the temple, with a priest at the hour of prayer, and he will end it in the temple, with the disciples “continually in the temple praising and blessing God” (Luke 24:53). He sets John’s birth beside Jesus’ birth, so that the forerunner and the Lord are announced by the same angel.

seeing.reveals: Gabriel says John will turn many to “the Lord their God” and go before Him. The One whose way John prepares is Jesus. From the first scene of Luke’s Gospel, the coming of Jesus is the coming of the Lord Himself to His people.
seeing.living: Zacharias was righteous and blameless, yet after years of disappointment he could not believe good news when it came. God disciplined his unbelief, but He did not cancel the promise. Bring God the prayers you have long carried, and do not demand proof before you let Him be faithful.
seeing.ponder: Is there a prayer you stopped praying because you decided God’s answer must be no?

preaching.big_idea: God hears long-unanswered prayers and keeps His promises, even when His servants struggle to believe.
outline: Faithful people with an empty home (5–7)
An answer at the hour of prayer (8–17)
A question that silenced a priest (18–22)
preaching.watch_for: The people were waiting for Zacharias, probably to receive the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26), but he came out unable to speak. Luke’s Gospel ends with Jesus lifting up His hands and blessing His disciples (Luke 24:50–51). The blessing the priest could not give, Jesus gives.
